comments.author: @kilanspeaks
comments.text:
What a brilliantly researched video! As an Indonesian, we learn about the Wallace Line (along with Weber and Lydekker) in school geography, but we rarely appreciate how insane it is until foreigners remind us. Most of us are just too caught up in the daily grind of survival (rawdogging apocalyptic natural disasters, dodging corrupt politicians, and running three side hustles) to step back and digest that we live in a country with tigers on one side and tree kangaroos on the other.

Outsiders also rarely grasp that across a landmass spanning the distance from London to Tehran, our human landscape is just as wildly diverse as the fauna. Phenotypes range from straight to tightly coiled hair, golden-wheat to deep dark skin, and neighboring ethnic groups can speak entirely different language families. 

Within the same borders, you have the Makassarese, renowned seafarers who traded with Indigenous Australians centuries before Europeans ever set foot there, alongside the Korowai, who build treehouses soaring 45 to 50 meters (148 to 164 feet) into the canopy. The biodiversity is only half the story.

replies.author: @anggitaputri3123
replies.text:
Im Indonesian and when I was an elementary students my teacher taught me there are three distinct fauna zones in Indonesia which is: 
1. Asian Zone (West), animals in island of Borneo, Sumatra, Java, and Bali: Sumatran Tiger, Bornean & Tapanuli Orangutan, Bekantan (Proboscis Monkey), Javan Rhinoceros, Sumatran Elephant and Kerbau (Carabao in Filipino/ Water Buffalo).
2. Transitional Zone (Central), animals in island of Sulawesi and Lesser Sunda islands : Babirusa (Deer-pig), Anoa (Wild Pygmy Buffalo), Tarsier, Komodo Dragon, Maleo Bird (Largest known egg-to-body ratio bird).
3. Australian Zone (East), animals in island of New Guinea and Moluccas: Cassowary, Tree Kangaroo, Echidna, and Cendrawasih (Bird of Paradise).
And these three zones are divided by Wallace and Weber Lines.
